notes.summary: These are clerical-speed questions: checking whether names, numbers, addresses and dates are exactly the same, reading letters from a number matrix, checking codes against rules, and putting names in index order. SSC asks 0 to 1 question. They need no formula, only a careful, chunk-by-chunk method.

concepts.title: What these questions test
concepts.body:
Government offices handle forms, registers and records all day. These questions check that you can spot a single wrong letter or digit quickly. The four common shapes:
  • Count how many pairs are exactly the same.
  • Pick the address or record identical to the one given.
  • Match a date or city written in a different format.
  • Decode letters from a matrix of row and column numbers.

concepts.title: Compare in small chunks
concepts.body:
Read 3 or 4 characters at a time from both items, using a pen as a pointer. Long numbers: split them the same way in both (457-3821 and 457-3281).
Common changeExample
Two digits swapped302015 / 302051
One vowel changed or addedKumar / Kumer, Kamla / Kamala
Letters that look alikeO / 0, I / 1 / l, rn / m, S / 5
Singular and pluralSilver Oaks / Silver Oak
Number order in an address24/B / 42/B, Sector 12 / Sector 21
Punctuation and spacingA-101 / A101, St. / St
Short formsArjun Mehta / Arjun M.
"Exactly the same" means every character, including dots, hyphens and spaces.

concepts.title: Matching addresses field by field
concepts.body:
Break the address into fields and compare one field across all options before moving on:
  1. Name
  2. House or flat number
  3. Building, street or sector
  4. Area and city
  5. PIN code (6 digits)
After each field, cross out options that differ. Usually one option survives within three fields. If the question asks "which entries are identical to each other", compare each entry with the first one, then group the ones that match.

concepts.title: Date formats
concepts.body:
Format5 November 1998
DD-MM-YYYY (India)05-11-1998
MM/DD/YYYY (USA)11/05/1998
YYYY-MM-DD (computers)1998-11-05
In words5 Nov 1998
Month numbers: 01 Jan, 02 Feb, 03 Mar, 04 Apr, 05 May, 06 Jun, 07 Jul, 08 Aug, 09 Sep, 10 Oct, 11 Nov, 12 Dec.
Days in a month: 31 in Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec; 30 in Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov; 28 in Feb (29 in a leap year). So 31-04-2023 is not a real date.
First find which part is the day and which is the month, then compare.

concepts.title: Cities, states and PIN codes
concepts.body:
The first digit of an Indian PIN code shows the region:
First digitRegion
1Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Chandigarh
2Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand
3Rajasthan, Gujarat
4Maharashtra, Goa, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh
5Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka
6Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry
7West Bengal, Odisha, the North-East
8Bihar, Jharkhand
9Army Postal Service
So "Jaipur – 302015" is consistent, but "Jaipur – 502015" is not.

concepts.title: Matrix indexing
concepts.body:
Letters are placed in a grid. Each letter is coded by its row number first, then its column number. If row 2, column 7 holds T, then T = 27.
  • Often two matrices are given: Matrix I uses rows and columns 0 to 4, Matrix II uses 5 to 9. The digits tell you which matrix to look in.
  • A letter can appear more than once, so it can have several codes. That is why options may look different but all be correct.
  • To find the right option, check one code per option until one fails. To find the wrong option ("which does NOT represent"), find the code that points to a different letter.

concepts.title: Code rules and roll numbers
concepts.body: Some questions describe how a valid code is built, for example: "2 capital letters for the state, then 4 digits for the year, a hyphen, then 5 digits". Check each option against every rule in order: length, capitals or small letters, digits in the right places, separators. One broken rule makes the code invalid. Count characters carefully; a missing digit is the most common difference.

concepts.title: Name indexing
concepts.body:
In an index or directory, names are listed by surname first, then the first name.
  • Rakesh Sharma is filed as "Sharma, Rakesh".
  • Same surname: sort by first name (Sharma, Anita before Sharma, Rakesh).
  • Titles such as Dr., Mr. and Smt. are ignored when sorting.
  • Initials come before full names that start with the same letter (Gupta, R. before Gupta, Rahul).
After you rewrite the names surname first, use normal dictionary order.

varieties.name: Identical pairs
varieties.how: Compare each pair in chunks of 3 or 4 characters, including punctuation. Mark each pair same or different, then count.

example.q:
How many pairs are exactly the same?
(1) 7804219 – 7804291
(2) Suresh Chand – Suresh Chand
(3) AB-2207-K – AB-2207-K
(4) 14/03/2021 – 14/08/2021
steps: (1) 780-4219 and 780-4291: the last two digits are swapped. Different.

varieties.name: Address matching
varieties.how: Split the address into fields (name, house number, street, city, PIN). Compare one field across all options and cross out any that differ.

example.q:
Which entries are identical to "Meenal Gupta, 102, Silver Oaks, Sector 12, Noida, 201301"?
1. Meenal Gupta, 102, Silver Oaks, Sector 12, Noida, 201301
2. Meenal Gupta, 102, Silver Oak, Sector 12, Noida, 201301
3. Meenal Gupta, 120, Silver Oaks, Sector 12, Noida, 201301
4. Meenal Gupta, 102, Silver Oaks, Sector 12, Noida, 201301
steps: House number: entry 3 has 120, not 102. Cross it out.
Building: entry 2 has "Silver Oak", not "Silver Oaks". Cross it out.
Entries 1 and 4 match in every field.

varieties.name: Date and city matching
varieties.how: Work out which part is the day, the month and the year in each format. Convert the given date into the asked format and compare.

example.q: A ticket shows 09/07/2024 in the Indian DD/MM/YYYY format. What will the same date look like in the US format MM/DD/YYYY?
steps: DD = 09, MM = 07, so the date is 9 July 2024.
In MM/DD/YYYY, the month comes first: 07/09/2024.

varieties.name: Matrix indexing
varieties.how: List every code of each letter (row first, then column). Check one code per option; reject an option as soon as one code points to a wrong letter.

example.q:
Each letter is coded as row number then column number. Which set gives RATE?
56789
0STARE
1MONET
2RATIO
(a) 08, 26, 19, 18 (b) 25, 07, 27, 17 (c) 08, 26, 28, 09 (d) 25, 16, 06, 09

varieties.name: Centre code and roll number rules
varieties.how: Turn the rules into a checklist (length, letters, digits, separators, capitals). Test each option against every rule; one failure makes it invalid.

example.q: A valid roll number has 2 capital letters, then 4 digits for the year, then a hyphen, then 5 digits. Which is valid? (a) UP2024-12345 (b) Up2024-12345 (c) UP224-12345 (d) UP2024-1234
steps: (c) has only 3 digits for the year. Invalid.
(d) has only 4 digits after the hyphen. Invalid.

varieties.name: Name indexing
varieties.how: Rewrite each name surname first. Sort by surname, then by first name, using dictionary order. Ignore titles.

example.q: Arrange as in a directory: 1. Rakesh Sharma 2. Anita Sharma 3. Vikas Gupta 4. Rahul Sinha
steps: Surname first: Sharma Rakesh, Sharma Anita, Gupta Vikas, Sinha Rahul.
Gupta comes first, then the two Sharmas, then Sinha.

tips: Read 3 or 4 characters at a time and move a pen along both items together.
Compare one field at a time across all options instead of reading each option fully.
Check numbers first; swapped digits are the most common difference.
In matrix questions, the row number always comes first.
For dates, first label day, month and year; 31 days never come in April, June, September or November.
In directory order, write the surname first before sorting.
traps: Similar spellings (Kamla and Kamala, Oak and Oaks) look the same at a glance.
Reading the column first in matrix codes.
Mixing up DD/MM and MM/DD: 05/11 is 5 November in India but May 11 in the US format.
Ignoring a missing hyphen, dot or space when the question asks for an exact match.

questions.q:
How many of the following pairs are exactly the same?
(1) 4573821 – 4573821
(2) Rajesh Kumar – Rajesh Kumer
(3) 12/09/2025 – 12/09/2025
(4) MNOPQ – MNOQP
questions.solution:
(1) Same.
(2) Kumar vs Kumer: different.
(3) Same.
(4) MNOPQ vs MNOQP: P and Q swapped, different.
So 2 pairs are the same.

questions.q:
Which option is exactly the same as the given address?
Anil Sharma, 24/B, Gandhi Nagar, Jaipur – 302015
questions.solution:
(a) PIN 302051 ≠ 302015.
(b) Exactly the same.
(c) Sarma ≠ Sharma.
(d) 42/B ≠ 24/B.

questions.q:
A word is represented by a set of numbers. Each letter is given by its row number followed by its column number in the matrix below. Which set represents the word MAP?
56789
0STARE
1MONET
2RATIO
3PLANS
4EMITS
A form shows a date of birth as 05-11-1998 (DD-MM-YYYY). Which of the following is the same date?
questions.solution:
DD = 05, MM = 11, YYYY = 1998.
Month 11 = November.
So the date is 5 November 1998.

questions.q:
Each letter is given by its row number followed by its column number in the matrix below. Which set does NOT represent the word RAT?
56789
0STARE
1MONET
2RATIO
3PLANS
4EMITS
questions.solution:
R = 08 or 25; A = 07, 26 or 37; T = 06, 19, 27 or 48.
(a) R, A, T ✓. (b) R, A, T ✓. (c) R, A, T ✓.
(d) 36 = row 3, column 6 = L, not T. So (d) does not represent RAT.

questions.q:
In how many of the following pairs are both entries exactly the same?
(1) 8920436 – 8920436
(2) Kamla Devi – Kamala Devi
(3) Plot 7/C, Sector 12 – Plot 7/C, Sector 21
(4) PQ-4471-ZX – PQ-4471-ZX
(5) 23.05.2019 – 23.05.2019
questions.solution:
(1) Same. (2) Kamla vs Kamala: different. (3) Sector 12 vs 21: different. (4) Same. (5) Same.
So 3 pairs are the same.

flashcards.back: Compare in chunks of 3–4 characters; watch swapped digits.
